subsection: 6. Energy value and dietary fibre targets

points: Carbohydrate provides 16 kJ (3.75 kcal) per gram; sugars and starch have the same energy value.
For comparison, protein provides 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram, fat 37 kJ (9 kcal) per gram and alcohol 29 kJ (7 kcal) per gram.
Fibre is not digested, so it contributes little usable energy.
Energy from a food is calculated by multiplying the grams of carbohydrate by 16 kJ, or by 3.75 kcal.
Worked example: 30 g of sugar provides 30 × 16 = 480 kJ, or 30 × 3.75 = 112.5 kcal.
Settings: a comparative study of the energy value of foods with and without added sugar, such as two breakfast cereals, using the carbohydrate and energy figures on their labels.
Settings: compare the energy in a food, such as a bar of chocolate, with the time an activity takes to use it up.

notes.h: Contribution of carbohydrates to the average diet
points: The Food Pyramid places bread, cereals, potatoes, rice and pasta at its base, so they should supply the largest share of the energy in the diet.
Foods with added sugar supply energy but few other nutrients, so they are described as energy-dense and nutrient-poor.
Replacing sugary foods with wholegrain starchy foods, fruit and vegetables raises the intake of fibre and vitamins.

notes.h: Dietary fibre: EFSA recommendation and how to meet it
points: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) recommends a daily intake of dietary fibre for adults, measured as non-starch polysaccharides.
Irish healthy eating guidance from the Department of Health and the Food Pyramid advises eating plenty of wholegrain cereals, fruit and vegetables every day.
Choose wholegrain or wholemeal bread, brown rice and wholemeal pasta in place of white versions.
Eat fruit and vegetables with their skins on, and bake or boil potatoes in their jackets, since most of the fibre in a potato is in the skin.
Add pulses such as beans, lentils and peas to soups, stews and salads.
Add seeds such as sunflower, pumpkin and linseed, bran or porridge oats to breakfast cereals, yoghurt and salads.
Check the fibre content per 100 g on the nutrition label when choosing breakfast cereals.
Snack on fresh fruit, dried fruit or a handful of nuts instead of biscuits or crisps.
Read ingredient lists: added sugars appear under names such as sucrose, glucose syrup, fructose, honey, cane sugar and fruit juice concentrate.
Choose reduced-sugar or sugar-free versions of drinks, jams, cereals and yoghurts.
Replace fizzy drinks with water or with fruit juice diluted with sparkling water.
Eat whole fruit rather than juices or smoothies, which contain less fibre.
Do not add sugar to tea, coffee or breakfast cereals; reduce the sugar in recipes and use spices, vanilla or ripe fruit for flavour.
Limit sweets, biscuits, cakes and sweet sauces, and keep fruit or vegetable sticks as snacks.
Tooth decay: bacteria in plaque ferment sugar to produce acid, which dissolves the enamel of the teeth.
Weight gain and obesity: sugary foods are energy-dense, so regular intake adds to excess energy intake.
Type 2 diabetes: a diet high in sugar and energy is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, which is linked to excess body weight.
Heart disease and high blood pressure: high sugar intake is associated with a higher risk of heart disease and raised blood pressure.
Nutritional deficiency: foods high in sugar displace fruit, vegetables and other nutrient-rich foods from the diet.
Intense sweeteners, such as aspartame and saccharin, are many times sweeter than sugar, so only tiny amounts are needed and they add almost no energy.
Bulk sweeteners, such as sorbitol, mannitol and xylitol, have a similar bulk to sugar and provide some energy.
Sorbitol and other bulk sweeteners act as humectants: they retain moisture and stop products drying out.
Sweeteners are used in low-calorie, sugar-free and diabetic foods, drinks and confectionery.
Sweeteners cannot replace all of sugar's functions: they do not provide the bulk, browning or preserving action of sugar.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of energy a food provides, measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal).
A unit of energy, commonly called a Calorie, equal to about 4.2 kilojoules.
The part of plant food made of non-starch polysaccharides that the human digestive system does not break down.
A plant polysaccharide, such as cellulose or pectin, that forms dietary fibre.
A sweetener that is many times sweeter than sugar and so is needed in very small amounts.
A sweetener, such as sorbitol, that has a similar bulk to sugar and provides some energy.
A substance that absorbs and holds moisture, keeping a food from drying out.
The Irish food guide that places bread, cereals, potatoes, rice and pasta at its base as the foods to eat most of.

factCards.term: Energy values per gram of protein, carbohydrate, fat and alcohol
factCards.definition: Protein 17 kJ (4 kcal), carbohydrate 16 kJ (3.75 kcal), fat 37 kJ (9 kcal) and alcohol 29 kJ (7 kcal).

factCards.term: Four effects of high sugar intake
factCards.definition: Tooth decay, weight gain and obesity, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease.

factCards.term: Four strategies for reducing sugar when preparing food
factCards.definition: Reduce the sugar in recipes, use spices, vanilla or ripe fruit for flavour, avoid adding sugar to drinks and cereals, and use unsweetened fruit in desserts.

questions.prompt: Calculate the energy provided by 40 g of starch, giving your answer in kilojoules and in kilocalories, and show your working.
questions.model: Energy value of carbohydrate: 16 kJ per gram. 40 × 16 = 640 kJ. Energy value of carbohydrate in kilocalories: 3.75 kcal per gram. 40 × 3.75 = 150 kcal.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the average diet can be adjusted to meet the EFSA fibre recommendation and reduce sugar intake, and evaluate the effects of a diet high in sugar on health.
questions.model: Fibre: swap white bread, rice and pasta for wholegrain versions; eat fruit and vegetables with skins on; add pulses to soups, stews and salads; add seeds, bran or porridge oats to cereals; choose high-fibre breakfast cereals and check the fibre per 100 g on the label; snack on fruit or nuts. Sugar: read ingredient lists for added sugars under names such as sucrose, glucose syrup, honey and fruit juice concentrate; choose reduced-sugar drinks and cereals; replace fizzy drinks with water or diluted juice; eat whole fruit rather than juice; do not add sugar to tea, coffee or cereals; limit sweets, biscuits and cakes. Effects of high sugar: tooth decay from acid produced by plaque bacteria; weight gain and obesity from energy-dense foods; type 2 diabetes; heart disease and high blood pressure; displacement of fruit, vegetables and other nutrient-rich foods, leading to nutritional deficiency. Sweeteners may reduce sugar and energy intake but cannot replace sugar's bulk, browning or preserving action.
